edits.find:
Torticollis has a direction, and the direction is the diagnosis. The sternocleidomastoid turns the head to the opposite side, so a shortened left muscle pulls the left ear toward the left shoulder and swings the chin right — exactly the geometry described, with the mass in the left sternocleidomastoid. The flat head is downstream: she can only look one way, so she lies on one spot.

The etiology is in the delivery note. Breech presentation means intrauterine crowding, the same mechanism that produces developmental dysplasia of the hip, metatarsus adductus and clubfoot. The non-transilluminating mass is the sentence written to stop you answering the neck lump instead of the syndrome.

The direction of the tilt identifies the side of the tight muscle. In this infant the mass is in the left sternocleidomastoid, which fits this pattern. The flat head is secondary: she can only look one way, so she lies on one spot.

Breech presentation points to intrauterine crowding as the cause. The same mechanism produces developmental dysplasia of the hip, metatarsus adductus and clubfoot. The non-transilluminating mass is part of the torticollis syndrome, not a separate neck lump.

edits.find:
Three reflexes localize a weak newborn arm. The Moro needs shoulder abduction and elbow extension (C5-C6) and a pain-free arm; the biceps reflex runs through C5-C6; the grasp runs through C8-T1. Here the grasp is absent while Moro and biceps are intact, the hand is clawed, and the same side has ptosis and miosis: a lower plexus (Klumpke, C8-T1) injury, with Horner syndrome because the sympathetic fibers to the eye leave the cord with T1.

Erb palsy (C5-C6) is the commonest birth palsy and the mirror image: Moro and biceps lost, grasp kept. A clavicle or humerus fracture lowers the Moro only through pain, keeps biceps and grasp, and has crepitus.

edits.find: Management ladder & the sling trap First-line is relative rest + physical therapy — strengthen the cuff and scapular stabilizers to open the subacromial space. "Rest" must never be communicated as immobilize: a sling causes atrophy and adhesive capsulitis, and slings are for dislocation and fracture only. No reflex MRI — X-ray only for trauma or failed therapy, and older adults have asymptomatic cuff tears on MRI. Subacromial steroid injection gives short-term relief only, and never through suspected infection.
edits.with: Management ladder & sling avoidance First-line is relative rest + physical therapy. Therapy strengthens the cuff and scapular stabilizers to open the subacromial space. "Rest" must never be communicated as immobilize. A sling causes atrophy and adhesive capsulitis; slings are for dislocation and fracture only. Do not order a reflex MRI (magnetic resonance imaging). Obtain an X-ray only for trauma or failed therapy. Older adults have asymptomatic cuff tears on MRI. Subacromial steroid injection gives short-term relief only and is never given through suspected infection.
